title: Design Spec: Workload-aware batching defaults (tiered profiles: fast / standard / cost-efficient)
author: Ethan Park
content:
## 1. Summary
This document specifies the end-to-end design for **tiered, workload-aware batching defaults** in Redwood Inference.

Customers (and internal Redwood services) will be able to select one of three batching tiers:
- **fast**: prioritize low queue delay and stable streaming cadence
- **standard**: balanced defaults (recommended general-purpose)
- **cost-efficient**: prioritize throughput and $/token improvements, with guardrails to avoid tail-latency and error-rate regressions

The system will:
1) expose tier selection across Hosted/Dedicated/Private config surfaces
2) map tier selection + workload signals into concrete runtime scheduler parameters
3) define clear **precedence rules** (explicit knobs override tier defaults)
4) provide an **effective config explain** output for debuggability and support
5) define **migration and rollout** strategy (feature flag, staged enablement, auto-rollback hooks)
6) handle edge cases (streaming, long-context, tool-calls, embeddings/rerank)

This is a productization/hardening effort; it does not introduce a novel scheduling algorithm.

---

## 2. Goals / Non-goals
### 2.1 Goals
- Define a minimal, stable customer-facing abstraction: `batching_tier` with 3 supported values.
- Provide safe-by-default parameters per tier with model-family and GPU-SKU override capability.
- Make tier behavior "workload-aware" using explicit, inspectable request/workload signals (prompt length buckets, streaming/non-streaming, concurrency signals).
- Preserve backwards compatibility: existing explicit batching settings continue to work unchanged.
- Provide telemetry necessary to validate tier adherence and support safe rollout (latency, queue delay, batch formation, GPU utilization, cancellations/timeouts).

### 2.2 Non-goals (initial release)
- Fully automated per-customer bespoke batching optimization beyond the three tiers.
- New scheduler research (we will tune existing knobs + add limited heuristics for workload awareness).
- Changing external API shapes in a breaking manner.

---

## 3. Terminology
- **Queue delay**: time from request arrival at runtime ingress to when it is admitted into a batch (prefill start).
- **Prefill**: compute phase processing prompt tokens.
- **Decode**: compute phase producing output tokens.
- **Continuous batching**: adding/removing sequences to a running batch across decode iterations.
- **Tier default**: a computed set of scheduler parameters derived from `batching_tier` + signals.
- **Explicit override**: customer-provided value for a concrete batching knob (e.g., `max_queue_delay_ms`) that overrides computed defaults.
- **Effective config**: final resolved knobs after applying precedence rules and model/GPU overrides.

---

## 4. User stories
1) As a developer, I want to set `batching_tier=fast` on my interactive chat route and get reliable p95 latency and stable streaming cadence without tuning.
2) As a platform engineer, I want `cost_efficient` on background summarization jobs to reduce $/token while staying within timeouts.
3) As SRE, I want per-tier dashboards (latency + queue delay + batch size distributions) and auto-rollback signals.
4) As Support/SE, I want a way to see the effective config and whether an explicit override is in effect.

---

## 5. Design overview
The implementation consists of five layers:

1) **Config surfaces**
   - Hosted API: request-level optional `batching_tier` (route-config default can be set in Console)
   - Dedicated: deployment config supports tier selection at route/model level
   - Private: helm values + control plane config supports tier selection

2) **Config schema & precedence**
   - Add `batching_tier` to runtime config schema
   - Keep existing explicit knobs (e.g., `max_batch_size`, `max_queue_delay_ms`, weights) with clear precedence

3) **Runtime selection logic**
   - Compute defaults using tier + workload signals + model/GPU override table
   - Enforce guardrails (clamps) and overload protection integration

4) **Explainability**
   - Surface `effective_batching_config` and provenance (which values came from tier, overrides, model defaults)

5) **Rollout & migration**
   - Feature flag gates tier-default computation and new UI surfaces
   - Staged rollout by model/region; auto-rollback hooks tied to SLO regressions

---

## 6. Config surfaces
### 6.1 Hosted API (request-level)
We support an optional request parameter `batching_tier` across chat/completions and (limited) embeddings.

**Request example (JSON)**
{
  "model": "rw-open-llama-3.1-70b",
  "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Summarize this..."}],
  "stream": true,
  "batching_tier": "fast"
}

Rules:
- If provided, request-level `batching_tier` takes precedence over route default tier.
- If omitted, route default tier is used.
- If neither request tier nor route tier is set, we behave as today (legacy defaults) until the feature is enabled by default.

### 6.2 Console / Control plane (route defaults)
Console will allow setting a default tier per route (chat/completions/embeddings/rerank) and per model selection. The UI must:
- Offer tier dropdown: fast / standard / cost-efficient
- Show computed effective defaults (read-only) and indicate which are overridden
- Link to docs and provide warnings for streaming + cost-efficient

### 6.3 Dedicated deployments
Dedicated customers often manage per-route config for predictable throughput. We support tier at:
- **deployment-wide default**
- **per route**
- **per model** (optional) 

Precedence (highest to lowest): request-level (if allowed) > route > model override > deployment default.

### 6.4 Private (VPC / on-prem)
Private deployments configure via helm + Redwood Private control plane.

**Helm values example (YAML)**
runtime:
  featureFlags:
    tieredBatchingDefaults: true
  routes:
    chat:
      defaultBatchingTier: standard
      overrides:
        - match:
            modelFamily: "llama3"
          batchingTier: fast

We will ship migration notes and validation rules to prevent invalid tier strings.

---

## 7. Runtime config schema
### 7.1 New field: batching_tier
Add an enum field to runtime config schema:
- `batching_tier`: one of `fast | standard | cost_efficient`

### 7.2 Explicit batching knobs (existing + normalized)
We keep existing explicit knobs. For the purpose of this spec, we reference the normalized internal names (the external names may be aliases):
- `max_batch_size`
- `max_queue_delay_ms`
- `max_prefill_tokens_per_batch`
- `max_decode_tokens_per_step`
- `prefill_weight` and `decode_weight` (or equivalent scheduler weights)
- `kv_cache_pressure_limit` (and associated thresholds)
- `admission_control`: thresholds for overload behavior (e.g., reject when queue delay exceeds limit)

### 7.3 Validation rules
- `batching_tier` must be valid enum.
- If explicit knobs are set, they must satisfy hard safety bounds (per model + GPU, where applicable). Examples:
  - `max_queue_delay_ms` must be within [0, 200] for `stream=true` requests unless explicitly allowed by elevated policy (internal only).
  - `max_batch_size` must not exceed runtime hard limit based on GPU memory estimation.

### 7.4 Backwards compatibility
- Existing configs without `batching_tier` behave unchanged.
- Existing explicit batching knobs continue to be honored; tier computation is skipped for any knob explicitly provided.

---

## 8. Precedence and effective config resolution
### 8.1 Precedence (per request)
For each request, we resolve the effective batching config using:

1) **Hard runtime limits** (non-overridable)
2) **Explicit request-level overrides** (if supported; initially tier only, not individual knobs)
3) **Explicit route/deployment config knobs** (customer-managed)
4) **Tier-derived defaults** (computed)
5) **Legacy defaults** (fallback for cases where tiering is disabled)

Important: tier selection itself can come from multiple levels (request vs route vs deployment). Once a tier is chosen, each knob is then computed unless explicitly set.

### 8.2 Example precedence scenario
- Route default tier: `standard`
- Customer sets explicit `max_queue_delay_ms=5` on the route
- Request sets `batching_tier=cost_efficient`

Outcome:
- Tier used for all knobs: cost_efficient
- `max_queue_delay_ms` remains 5 (explicit override)
- Other knobs (e.g., `max_batch_size`, weights) come from cost_efficient mapping

### 8.3 Effective config provenance
Runtime must attach provenance metadata (for explain endpoint and debugging):
- `source=tier` (include tier name)
- `source=explicit_override` (include config path)
- `source=model_registry_default` (include version)
- `source=runtime_hard_limit` (include clamp info)

---

## 9. Workload-aware selection logic
### 9.1 Inputs
Workload signals used by tier mapping must be explicit and logged:
- `is_streaming` (boolean)
- `route_type` (chat/completions/embeddings/rerank)
- `prompt_length_bucket` (e.g., 0–256, 257–1k, 1k–4k, 4k–16k, >16k)
- `expected_output_tokens_bucket` (if available)
- `concurrency_signal` (approx: active requests per replica / per GPU)
- `model_family` and `model_variant` (including quantization profile)
- `gpu_sku` (A100-80G, H100-80G, L40S, etc.)

Non-inputs (initial): tenant identity (except via rollout controls), prompt content, customer-specific heuristics.

### 9.2 Tier mapping functions
At a high level:
- `fast`: minimize queue delay; smaller batches; prioritize decode to preserve streaming cadence.
- `standard`: moderate queue delay; moderate batches; balanced prefill/decode weights.
- `cost_efficient`: allow larger batches and slightly higher queue delay (especially non-streaming); bias prefill batching; rely on overload protection + admission control to prevent runaway tail latency.

### 9.3 Baseline parameter table (illustrative; final values per model/GPU from registry)
The runtime will compute defaults from a table keyed by:
- tier
- streaming vs non-streaming
- prompt length bucket
- model family
- GPU SKU

Example baseline defaults for a common chat model family on H100-80G:

| Tier | Streaming | max_queue_delay_ms | max_batch_size | prefill_weight:decode_weight | Notes |
|------|-----------|--------------------|----------------|------------------------------|------|
| fast | true | 2 | 8 | 1:3 | protect token cadence |
| fast | false | 3 | 12 | 1:2 | minimize time-to-first-token |
| standard | true | 6 | 16 | 1:2 | balanced |
| standard | false | 8 | 24 | 2:2 | balanced throughput |
| cost_efficient | true | 10 (clamped) | 24 | 2:2 | must maintain cadence guardrail |
| cost_efficient | false | 15 | 48 | 3:1 | maximize batching |

Notes:
- Streaming queue delay values are intentionally low and may be further lowered for specific models.
- `cost_efficient` on streaming is allowed but more constrained (guardrails below).

### 9.4 Guardrails and clamps
To keep behavior safe-by-default:
- Clamp `max_queue_delay_ms` for streaming to a tier-specific maximum (e.g., fast<=3, standard<=8, cost_efficient<=12), subject to SRE review.
- Enforce `min_decode_priority` for streaming so decode is not starved by prefill batching.
- Apply KV cache pressure limits per tier to avoid OOM on cost_efficient under high concurrency.
- Admission control ties to queue delay and memory pressure:
  - if estimated queue delay would exceed `queue_delay_reject_threshold_ms`, reject early with a clear reason code (and increment counters)
  - for Dedicated/Private, optionally enable backpressure mode (429/503 with retry-after) rather than timeouts

---

## 10. Model registry and overrides
### 10.1 Why overrides live in the model registry
Some parameters must vary by model family/variant and sometimes by GPU SKU. Storing tier defaults in the model registry provides:
- versioning and auditability
- safe rollout toggles
- consistent behavior across Hosted/Dedicated/Private

### 10.2 Override layering
Default resolution order:
1) runtime base table (built-in)
2) model registry overrides by model family
3) model registry overrides by (model family + GPU SKU)
4) model registry overrides by (specific model version)

Constraints:
- registry overrides may only adjust an allowlisted set of knobs (ADR-041).
- all overrides must pass validation and perf canary gates before global rollout.

---

## 11. Edge cases
### 11.1 Streaming (chat/completions)
Risks:
- increased queue delay increases time-to-first-token
- aggressive prefill batching can degrade token cadence and perceived responsiveness

Behavior:
- `is_streaming=true` forces stricter bounds on queue delay and enforces decode-priority floor.
- `fast` tier must target smooth cadence; if the runtime is under load, prefer load-shedding/backpressure over accumulating queue delay.

Testing requirements:
- streaming cadence KPI: inter-token time p95 and long gaps (>250ms) frequency must not regress beyond thresholds defined in performance standards.

### 11.2 Long-context requests
Long prompts (e.g., >16k tokens) have heavy prefill cost and can dominate batch formation.

Behavior:
- For long-context buckets, reduce `max_batch_size` and/or set `max_prefill_tokens_per_batch` lower to prevent head-of-line blocking.
- Prefer grouping by prompt length bucket to avoid mixing very long prefill with many short requests when queue delay constraints would be violated.

### 11.3 Tool calling / structured output
Tool calling often involves:
- longer prompts (function schemas)
- multi-step tool loops
- stricter latency expectations for “interactive” behavior

Behavior:
- If request indicates tool-calling mode (via route metadata), default tier is recommended `fast` or `standard`; `cost_efficient` may be allowed but will be clamped similarly to streaming.
- Ensure cancellation handling is correct: tool loops may cancel intermediate generations; batching must account for higher cancel rate to avoid wasted compute.

### 11.4 Embeddings and rerank
Embeddings/rerank workloads are typically non-streaming and benefit from batching.

Behavior:
- Allow `cost_efficient` with larger `max_batch_size` and larger queue delay, within request timeout limits.
- For embeddings, prompt length distribution differs; we use separate baseline tables.

### 11.5 Mixed workloads on a shared pool
Shared hosted pools will mix tenants and routes. Risks include tail latency on interactive routes when background workloads use cost-efficient.

Mitigations:
- Route-level tier defaults should be enforced; interactive chat routes default to standard/fast.
- Admission control integrates with priority classes so interactive routes have preferential scheduling.

---

## 12. Explainability / debugging surfaces
### 12.1 Effective config endpoint
The runtime must provide an "explain" response for a given request context (or a sampled request) that returns:
- resolved tier
- resolved knobs (effective values)
- provenance per knob
- relevant signals used (streaming, prompt bucket, concurrency bucket, model family, GPU SKU)

**Example (conceptual output)**
- effective.batching_tier=standard (source=route_default)
- effective.max_queue_delay_ms=6 (source=tier)
- effective.max_batch_size=16 (source=model_registry_default v2025.03.10)
- effective.prefill_weight=1 (source=tier)
- effective.decode_weight=2 (source=tier)
- effective.max_queue_delay_ms clamped? false

This data is required for Console display and CS troubleshooting.

### 12.2 Response headers (Hosted API)
For Hosted API, we will optionally include headers for debugging (behind a support/debug flag):
- `x-rw-batching-tier-effective`
- `x-rw-batching-config-version`
- `x-rw-batching-overrides-present=true|false`

---

## 13. Telemetry requirements
Instrumentation must support tier validation and safe rollout.

Required metrics (tagged/labelled by tier, model, region, route, streaming):
- latency: p50/p95/p99 end-to-end
- queue delay histogram
- batch size histogram (prefill and decode)
- batch wait time
- prefill latency vs decode latency breakdown
- GPU utilization (SM, memory, KV cache)
- cancel/timeout rates and reason codes
- overload events: load-shed count, backpressure count, admission reject count

Tracing:
- spans for queue wait, prefill, decode
- attach effective tier and key knobs as span attributes for tail analysis

---

## 14. Migration strategy
### 14.1 Phase 0: schema addition (no behavior change)
- Add `batching_tier` field to schemas and SDK typing.
- Default behavior remains legacy unless the feature flag is enabled.

### 14.2 Phase 1: feature-flagged tier mapping
- Enable tier mapping behind `tiered_batching_defaults` flag.
- Only opt-in models/regions at first.

### 14.3 Phase 2: Console + docs
- Expose tier selection in Console with clear warnings and computed defaults.
- Ship docs and SDK examples.

### 14.4 Phase 3: staged default enablement
- For selected models/regions, set route default tier to `standard` (unless customer has explicit knobs configured).
- Keep ability to opt out to legacy defaults (time-bound during beta).

---

## 15. Rollout plan (high level)
- Start with internal dogfood in one region and 1–2 popular models.
- Expand to a limited customer beta cohort (opt-in).
- Ramp by percentage (by model+region) with canary checks and automatic rollback triggers.

Rollback triggers (examples; final thresholds in SRE doc):
- p95 latency regression beyond tier budget for 15 min window
- timeout rate increase above threshold
- streaming cadence regression (inter-token gap spikes)
- GPU OOM / memory pressure alarms increased

---

## 16. Testing and evaluation
### 16.1 Perf canary
Perf canary must benchmark all three tiers across:
- top models (by traffic)
- key GPU SKUs
- representative workloads (prompt length histograms + concurrency sweeps)

Gates:
- p95 regression thresholds per tier
- streaming cadence checks
- queue delay distribution checks

### 16.2 Quality guardrails
Batching changes can affect sampling behavior and timing. We will run prompt-set quality checks (Applied ML) comparing:
- legacy baseline vs tier defaults
- last known good tier config vs new tier config

Quality gating criteria live in the guardrails doc; the runtime rollout uses those results as a go/no-go input.

### 16.3 E2E integration tests
- Verify tier selection precedence across chat/completions/embeddings routes
- Verify explicit knob overrides take effect and are reported in explain output
- Verify invalid tier strings are rejected with clear error messages

---

## 17. Operational considerations
### 17.1 SRE ownership
- SLO definitions per tier are owned by SRE (Sean Gallagher) and enforced via dashboards + alerts.
- On-call playbook must include: where to find effective config, key metrics, and rollback steps.

### 17.2 Supportability
Support workflows require:
- "effective config" visibility
- clear error codes (admission reject vs timeout vs capacity)
- guidance on when to switch tiers vs when to override a specific knob

---

## 18. Open questions
1) Request-level tier in Dedicated/Private: do we allow per-request tier override for customers, or restrict to route configuration initially?
2) Tier naming: do we stick with `cost_efficient` everywhere vs customer-facing “Cost-efficient”? (Implementation uses `cost_efficient`.)
3) How do we represent tool-calling signal consistently across routes (metadata vs explicit flag) without leaking product-specific semantics into runtime?
4) Do we need a fourth internal-only tier for benchmarking/extremes (not customer visible)?

---

## 19. Appendix
### 19.1 Tier enum values (canonical)
- `fast`
- `standard`
- `cost_efficient`

### 19.2 Error handling
Invalid tier value:
- Hosted API: 400 with message "Invalid batching_tier. Expected one of: fast, standard, cost_efficient"
- Control plane: validation error shown in Console and blocked on save

### 19.3 Change management
Any change to tier defaults (base tables or registry overrides) must include:
- perf canary run links
- quality eval report link
- rollout plan (percentage + models/regions)
- explicit rollback thresholds

(See ADR-041 and Performance Standards for required artifacts.)
